Pied-à-terre tax · Questions

What is New York City's pied-à-terre tax?

Short answers to the questions people search for, with the rates, the exemptions and the dates.

What is the pied-à-terre tax?

It is a yearly surcharge on expensive New York City homes that are nobody's primary residence. The law calls it a non-primary residence surcharge (Tax Law Article 30-C). It is added to the property tax bill.

What does pied-à-terre mean?

A pied-à-terre is a second home kept in a city for occasional stays. The tax uses the idea more broadly: any covered home that is not the primary residence of the owner, a close relative, or a long-term tenant.

Who has to pay it?

Owners of condos and co-ops with a city market value of $1 million or more, and of one- to three-family houses valued at $5 million or more, unless the home is a primary residence under the law's test.

How much is it?

For condos and co-ops in Phase 1: 4% of the whole city market value from $1 million to $3 million, 5.25% up to $5 million and 6.5% above. For houses: 0.8% from $5 million to $15 million, 1.05% up to $25 million and 1.3% above.

Is the value the sale price?

No. The city values condos and co-ops as if they were rental buildings, so the city value is usually far below the sale price. A $5 million condo can have a city value under $1 million.

Who is exempt?

The surcharge is not owed when the home is the primary residence of the owner, the owner's spouse, child, parent, sibling, grandparent or grandchild, or a tenant or subtenant on a bona fide arm's-length lease of at least one year. Residence is tested on January 5 of the calendar year before the tax year. Owning through an LLC or trust does not by itself make a home anyone's primary residence. Other exemptions and abatements do not reduce the surcharge (Tax Law § 1354(a)).

What about combined apartments?

The city values each tax lot separately. If two apartments were combined into one home but are still two tax lots, each lot has its own city value, and each can sit under $1 million even when the home is worth more. The Tax Commission asks owners to appeal a combined apartment as one residence. The Department of Finance rules do not say how the threshold applies to combined lots, so check the notice for each lot.

When is it due?

The first bills are on property tax statements due January 1, 2027.

How do I challenge it?

To contest the market value, file Tax Commission Form TC107 by March 1, 2027 for condos and co-ops or March 15, 2027 for houses. Residency is decided by the Department of Finance and can also be appealed.

What did the courts decide?

On November 4, 2026 a state appeals court dismissed a homeowners' suit over how the city sent its notices, finding the owners had not shown harm. Two other suits that challenge the tax itself are still pending.

What changes in 2028?

From July 1, 2028, condos and co-ops are valued from comparable sales, and the threshold for them rises to $5 million with the same 0.8% to 1.3% rates as houses.

Deadline to challenge the value

To contest the market value behind the surcharge, file Tax Commission Form TC107 by March 1, 2027 for condos and co-ops, or March 15, 2027 for houses. The form cannot be used to protest the assessed value. See the TC107 guide.
